title: Pediatric DKA: the first six hours

bedside.infusions: Insulin {insRate} U/kg/h. Fluid plan running: {fluidOn|yesno}. Potassium in the fluid: {kAdded|yesno}. Dextrose in the fluid: {not isNull(dexAt)|yesno}.

banner.text: Off the unit for a head CT.

objective: Recognize cerebral edema in DKA -- headache, falling heart rate, rising blood pressure, declining consciousness, new incontinence -- and treat with mannitol or hypertonic saline without waiting for a CT
secondaryObjectives: Resuscitate a child in DKA with isotonic fluid first, replace the remaining deficit gradually, then start a weight-based continuous insulin infusion without a bolus
Add dextrose to IV fluids as glucose falls during DKA treatment, and overlap subcutaneous insulin before stopping the infusion
Monitor potassium and phosphate during DKA treatment, because insulin drives both into cells
Apply the biochemical criteria for pediatric DKA (hyperglycemia, venous acidosis or low bicarbonate, and ketosis) and grade its severity by the acidosis

sources.cite: AACN Certification Corporation. CCRN Exam Handbook - Direct Care (July 2026), Pediatric test plan
sources.note: The objective and its secondary objectives are the course's own titles (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/ccrn-peds-neo.ts, read there from the handbook 2026-10-31). Not re-fetched for this scenario.

sources.cite: Glaser N, Fritsch M, Priyambada L, Rewers A, Cherubini V, Estrada S, Wolfsdorf JI, Codner E. ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state. Pediatr Diabetes 2022;23:835-856
sources.note: Primary text read 2026-11-11 (a hosted copy of the published chapter): DKA needs glucose >200 mg/dL, venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <18 and ketosis; severe is pH <7.1 or bicarbonate <5; initial 0.9% saline 10-20 mL/kg over 20-30 min, deficit replaced over 24-48 h; insulin 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h starting 1 h after fluids begin, 'An IV insulin bolus should not be used at the start of therapy'; potassium 40 mmol/L in the fluid once K is below 5.5, insulin deferred for a low K (the executive summary says <3.0, section 6.3.4 says <3.5: the text is inconsistent); 5% dextrose added at about 250-300 mg/dL, or sooner if glucose falls faster than 90 mg/dL (5 mmol/L) per hour; expected fall 2-5 mmol/L (36-90 mg/dL) per hour; glucose hourly, electrolytes every 2-4 h, hourly vital signs and neurological checks; cerebral injury usually within 12 h of starting treatment; major signs altered mentation, sustained heart rate fall of more than 20 not explained by volume or sleep, age-inappropriate incontinence; minor signs vomiting, headache, lethargy, diastolic BP >90; mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg over 10-15 min (effect from about 15 min, lasting about 120 min) or 3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg over 10-15 min; 'treatment of the clinically symptomatic patient should not be delayed in order to obtain imaging'; bicarbonate not recommended except for life-threatening hyperkalemia or pH below 6.9 with compromised contractility; PECARN FLUID found no difference in cerebral injury between faster and slower rehydration.

brief.situation: Handover at 20:00 in the pediatric ICU. Bed 3, a 9-year-old boy, 30 kg, new-onset type 1 diabetes. Two weeks of thirst and weight loss, vomiting today. ED venous gas: pH 7.06, bicarbonate 7, glucose 560 mg/dL, potassium 4.6, ketones high. The ED gave 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline from 19:30 to 20:00. Insulin is ordered at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h; it has not started.
handover: HR 118, BP 108/66, RR 32 and deep, SpO2 99% on room air. Awake, tired, answers questions. GCS 15.
Warm hands, capillary refill 2 s. He passed urine in the ED.
Orders: deficit and maintenance fluid over 48 hours, potassium 40 mmol/L in the fluid once K is below 5.5 and he is passing urine, hourly glucose and neuro checks, gas and electrolytes every 2 hours.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Results take minutes; hourly checks are waits you can skip to. The skip stops early at an alarm or a result.
Look at the child yourself: some changes show on the monitor before anyone tells you.
Partway through you are asked to write your plan. The case ends at the six-hour review, then a debrief scores what you did.

plan.trigger: not isNull(insAt) and t >= timeAt(insAt) + reasonDelay
plan.question: Insulin is running. What will you watch for over the next hours, and what would you do about each?

parts.label: Severity and the plan
parts.criteria: Grades this as severe DKA (pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5; here pH 7.06) and states the plan: fluid deficit over 24-48 h, insulin 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h without a bolus started an hour after fluids, potassium in the fluid, dextrose added as glucose falls toward 250-300 while insulin continues.
parts.modelAnswer: Severe DKA by the acidosis (pH 7.06). Fluids replace the deficit over 48 hours, insulin runs at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h with no bolus from an hour after fluids began, potassium goes in the fluid because insulin drives it into cells, and dextrose goes in when glucose reaches about 250-300 so the insulin can keep clearing ketones.

parts.label: What to watch for
parts.criteria: Names cerebral edema with at least three warning signs (headache, falling heart rate, rising diastolic pressure, falling GCS, new incontinence, vomiting) and the response: hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or 3% saline) at once without waiting for imaging; also hypokalemia and hypoglycemia with hourly glucose and electrolytes every 2-4 h.
parts.modelAnswer: Cerebral edema: a new headache, a heart rate that falls without reason, a rising diastolic, a dropping GCS or new incontinence. If I see that, call and give mannitol or 3% saline straight away, not after a CT. Also low potassium (electrolytes every 2 hours) and low glucose (hourly).

source.note: Attending called within 15 min of the first sign of cerebral edema.

noProgress.rationale: Cerebral edema left long enough to reach a GCS of about 9 has injured the brain even if he is waking at six hours, so this case calls it harm.

source.cite: Glaser N, Fritsch M, Priyambada L, Rewers A, Cherubini V, Estrada S, Wolfsdorf JI, Codner E. ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state. Pediatr Diabetes 2022;23:835-856
source.note: Cerebral injury mortality 21%-24% (ISPAD). The class choice is the author's, per docs/sims.md 9.2.

herniation.label: Brain herniation
herniation.narrative: His pupils became unequal and his breathing irregular, and his heart rate slowed further: the brain swelling has caused herniation. The team intubates; the outlook is grave.

arrhythmia.label: Arrhythmia from low potassium
arrhythmia.narrative: Ventricular ectopy, then a run of ventricular tachycardia: the insulin drove his potassium down to {k|1dp} with nothing replacing it.

resolving.label: Cerebral edema caught and treated; DKA resolving
resolving.when: t >= reviewAt and ceMax < injuryAt and not isNull(osmoAt) and timeAt(osmoAt) <= ceOnset + ceWindow and isNull(ctAt) and kAdded and (isNull(insAt) or timeAt(kAt) <= timeAt(insAt) + 3600) and not insBolus and not isNull(insAt) and timeAt(insAt) >= insStartMin and (isNull(needDexAt) or (not isNull(dexAt) and timeAt(dexAt) <= timeAt(needDexAt) + 3600)) and not insStopped and not lowGlu
resolving.narrative: Six hours in he is awake, GCS {gcs}, the headache settling. Hyperosmolar therapy went in within minutes of the first sign, without a trip to CT, and the DKA is resolving with insulin, potassium and dextrose in the right order.

resolvingLate.label: Alive and improving, by a slower route
resolvingLate.narrative: He is improving at six hours, but something cost time or safety: a late or CT-delayed treatment of the edema, an insulin bolus or early start, potassium late, a stopped insulin, or a low glucose.

time_up.label: Neurological injury
time_up.narrative: Six hours in he is waking, GCS {gcs}, but the swelling went untreated long enough to drop his GCS to about {15 - round(7 * ceMax)}: an MRI and a neurology review will show what it cost him.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: severity, the plan and the warning signs

kpis.label: Insulin started
kpis.expert: 30 min after handover (1 h after fluids)

expertPath.text: Neuro check (GCS 15), glucose, gas and electrolytes. Start the 48-hour fluid plan; K is 4.6 and he is passing urine, so add potassium 40 mmol/L.
An hour after fluids began: insulin 0.1 U/kg/h, no bolus.
Glucose and neuro checks every hour, gas and electrolytes every 2 hours. Add 5% dextrose when glucose is about 300, insulin unchanged.
New headache and vomiting: neuro check now. Heart rate falling, diastolic rising, GCS down, incontinent. Call the attending naming cerebral edema; mannitol or 3% saline at once. No CT first.

herniation.headline: Herniation from untreated cerebral edema
herniation.body: Find the first sign in the log (the headache at 00:20), then when the neuro check, the call and the hyperosmolar dose happened. A CT trip or waiting for the next hourly check costs the minutes that matter.

arrhythmia.headline: Arrhythmia from low potassium
arrhythmia.body: Insulin drives potassium into cells. It belongs in the fluid from the start once K is below 5.5 and he is passing urine, with electrolytes every 2-4 hours.

resolving.headline: Cerebral edema caught and treated
resolving.body: The warning signs were recognized at the bedside and treated within minutes, without waiting for imaging, and the DKA plan ran in the right order. That is the expert path.

resolvingLate.headline: Improving, by a slower route
resolvingLate.body: He is better, but check when the edema was treated and whether a CT came first, when potassium went in, whether insulin was bolused, started early or stopped, and whether his glucose fell low.

time_up.headline: Neurological injury
time_up.body: The edema was treated, but late. Every minute between the first sign and the dose matters; the signs are clinical, and the dose comes before any scan.

scoring.modelReasoning: Severe DKA (pH below 7.1) in a child with new type 1 diabetes. Isotonic fluid first, then the deficit over 24-48 h; insulin 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h from an hour after fluids begin, never as a bolus; potassium in the fluid once K is below 5.5 and urine is flowing, because insulin drives it into cells; 5% dextrose when glucose reaches about 250-300 so insulin can continue until the acidosis clears. Hourly glucose and neuro checks, electrolytes every 2-4 h. Cerebral edema usually appears within 12 h of starting treatment: headache, vomiting, a heart rate that falls without reason, a rising diastolic, declining consciousness, new incontinence. Treat it at once with mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg or 3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg over 10-15 min and call for help; imaging comes after, never before. Bicarbonate is not used.

noBolus.ask: While the labs run: should the insulin start with an IV bolus to bring the glucose down faster?

choices.label: No: an infusion only, no bolus

noBolus.explain: No. ISPAD says an IV insulin bolus should not be used at the start of therapy. The infusion at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/h starts an hour after fluids begin.

source.cite: Glaser N, Fritsch M, Priyambada L, Rewers A, Cherubini V, Estrada S, Wolfsdorf JI, Codner E. ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state. Pediatr Diabetes 2022;23:835-856
source.note: Quoted: 'An IV insulin bolus should not be used at the start of therapy.'

dexNotStop.ask: If this glucose comes back at 280 while the pH is still 7.18, what is the right move?

choices.label: Add dextrose and keep the insulin running
Stop the insulin until the glucose rises

dexNotStop.explain: Add dextrose and keep the insulin going. The insulin is there to clear the ketoacidosis, which lasts longer than the high glucose; dextrose at about 250-300 mg/dL lets it continue safely.

source.cite: Glaser N, Fritsch M, Priyambada L, Rewers A, Cherubini V, Estrada S, Wolfsdorf JI, Codner E. ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state. Pediatr Diabetes 2022;23:835-856
source.note: Add 5% dextrose at about 14-17 mmol/L (250-300 mg/dL), or sooner if glucose falls faster than 5 mmol/L per hour.

noCt.ask: While the attending calls back: should he go to CT before hyperosmolar therapy?

choices.label: No: treat now, image later if needed

noCt.explain: Treat now. Cerebral edema in DKA is a clinical diagnosis; ISPAD says treatment of the symptomatic child should not be delayed to obtain imaging, and an early CT may look normal.
